---
title: "News"
---

Major changes to the IRW — new data, new tools, and changes to what the
warehouse claims about itself. Smaller day-to-day work (individual table
additions, corrections to single tables, item-text disclosures) is not listed
here; see [Corrections](corrections.qmd) for every correction to a published
table, [Known Issues](itemtext_issues.qmd) for the running record of item-text
caveats, and the [GitHub repositories](https://github.com/ben-domingue/irw)
for everything else.

This log begins in September 2026, when the page was created. The IRW is older
than the log, and changes before then are recorded only in the repositories'
commit history and in the versioned data itself.

## 2026-10-05 — ENEM 2024 and 2025 ids corrected

Released 2026-10-05, across the eight `enem_2024_1mil_*` and `enem_2025_1mil_*`
tables and their eight `_nom` companions. From 2024 INEP ships participant and
results data as two separate files, keyed differently, and the year scripts had
taken `id` from one file and the responses from the other, pairing them by row
order. The test municipality in the two files agrees no more often than chance
would predict, so in effect every response sat under the wrong candidate's id.

`id` now comes from the results file's own `NU_SEQUENCIAL`. The candidates and
the `resp` and `resp_raw` sequences are unchanged row for row; only the id a
response carries is different. [Data Notes](data_notes.qmd) records one caveat:
`NU_SEQUENCIAL` is unique within a year but should not be used to follow a
person between years. 2013 to 2023 are untouched. Refs #2812.

## 2026-10-05 — The packages will tell you what a column means

Python package 0.4.0 through 0.7.3. `describe_columns` is a new MCP tool: for a
table it reports each column with the data standard's definition where the
standard defines it, the source column the build script renamed it from, a
covariate's value labels in the source's own words, and the source deposit's own
codebook or questionnaire where one has been found. `covariate_labels()` joins
the public Python API. The R package has `irw_covariate_labels()` and
`irw_covariates(labels = TRUE)` on main, but the released R package is still
1.3.0, so there they are merged and not yet shipped. Setup for the MCP server is
on [Using an AI Assistant](agents.qmd).

## 2026-10-04 — Every table page now has a Codebook section

The plain Columns list on a table page has become a Codebook: one row per
column, giving the data standard's definition where it defines the column, and
the source column the build script renamed it from, linked to the line that
renames it. Covariates list their labelled codes in code order and in the
source's own words ("1 = hombre · 2 = mujer"). Where the source deposit's own
codebook was found, the section links it, and links a questionnaire beside it
when the codebook names the columns but not the response wording.

The section says it is the IRW's best reconstruction rather than the source's
codebook, that it may contain mistakes, and that the source data are the
authority. It never infers a meaning from a column's name: a column with neither
a definition nor a traced source is shown as not documented. Refs #2755, #2763,
#2766, #2770, #2787, #2792.

## 2026-10-03 — Non-commercial and GPL licences now proceed

A ruling of 2026-10-01, now in the processing repo's data standard: a
non-commercial licence is hostable, with the NC carried into the derived
licence, and so is GPL. ND licences and scraped or relabelled third-party data
still stop, and a dataset with no licence at all still means asking the author
for permission. The intake-policy section of [the data standard](standard.qmd)
on this site has not yet caught up. Refs #2808, #2809.

## 2026-10-03 — The homepage counts the published warehouse, and Standards gets its own menu

The front-page banner is now rebuilt from published `irw_meta` on every render
and records the version it read, where before it came from a file committed by
hand and lagged what was published. It also gives the competition and nominal
table counts. Refs #1940.

The Data menu split in two. Data holds the pages for using the tables, with
[Corrections](corrections.qmd) moved over from About; Standards holds the
specifications, the validator and the contributing guidance, with
[Overview of the IRW Data Standards](overview.qmd) as its hub.

## 2026-10-02 — The standard defines design columns, and `irw-validate` 1.4.0

`cluster_id`, `block_id` and `std_baseline*` are now defined in the standard's
schema table, its column order and its section on randomised trials; until now
the validator told the tables carrying them, such as the `gilbert_*` series, to
rename them as covariates. `irw-validate` 1.4.0 allows them, and demotes its
composite-item check to a warning, since label names alone cannot establish that
a column holds a computed score. The standard also now says the 100-respondent
floor does not apply to animal data, and clause C4 has an exception for
IEA-style sources: an omitted response is scored 0 with the source's code kept
in `resp_raw`, while a not-reached response is dropped. The
[browser validator](validate.qmd) runs 1.4.0 too.

## 2026-10-01 — Competition, nominal and simulated data all grew

`irw_competitions` (v6.2) now covers professional and historical sport, machine
contests such as chess engines and Kaggle simulation competitions, animal
dominance hierarchies, comparative judgement and quiz contests; see
[the competition standard](comps_standard.qmd). `irw_nominal` (v3.3) and
`irw_simsyn` (v1.4) grew as well; see [the nominal standard](nominal_standard.qmd)
and [simulated and synthetic data](simsyn.qmd).

## 2026-10-01 — A measured quantity is not a response

Ruled over the week and recorded on [Corrections](corrections.qmd): the
`continuous_response` collection is for response scales — sliders, 0–100
ratings, visual analogue scales — and a physical measurement such as minutes,
hours or amount consumed never belongs in it. Self-reported counts stay.
Refs #1700.

## 2026-09-30 — Corrections from the corpus audit

The retroactive audit of the existing corpus published its first large batch of
corrections on 2026-09-30, each listed on [Corrections](corrections.qmd) with
the version it took effect in. The audit works by class rather than by table —
sentinel codes stored as responses, covariates out of range, response times in
the wrong units, binary scales carrying extra codes, exact duplicate rows — so a
defect found in one table is then looked for everywhere. Refs #2401.

## 2026-09-30 — Eedi NeurIPS licence corrected

Eedi permitted the IRW to reshare its restructured NeurIPS 2020 and 2022 data on
condition that it carry CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, and the dictionary and bibliography had
recorded CC BY 4.0. The rows for `neurips_2020`, `neurips_2020_task34` and
`neurips_2022` now state the licence the permission actually granted.

## 2026-09-30 — Twenty-one collections for specific instruments

Collections were added for the PHQ-9, GAD-7, RSES, SWLS, PSS-10, DASS-21,
PANAS, CES-D, BFI-44, BFI-10, TIPI, SD3, ERQ, GSE, MSPSS, Brief COPE, PCL-5,
LOT-R, ISI, FCV-19S and the UCLA Loneliness Scale. Unlike the tag-based
collections, these are curated table by table, and every member records its
basis — whether the instrument was identified from the item wording, from what
the source supplied, or only from the table's name.
[Browse IRW Collections](collections.qmd) lists them member by member, with the
basis shown and filterable.

## 2026-09-28 — Source caveats get a Notes section, and a page

A note is not a correction: it describes something odd about a source that the
IRW table reproduces faithfully, rather than a defect in the IRW's own
processing. Notes now appear as a plain Notes section on a table page, under
"About this table", and the new [Data Notes](data_notes.qmd) page lists all of
them. Because a note is about the source and not about the IRW's handling of it,
it carries no banner and does not keep a table out of search results.

## 2026-09-28 — The MCP server can find the script that built a table

Python package 0.3.1. The server's processing-notes tool now resolves a table
to the script that produced it through a table-to-script index generated in the
processing repo, instead of guessing at a path. If you use the local MCP server
described on [Using an AI Assistant](agents.qmd), an assistant can now ask how
a particular table was built and get the actual script.

## 2026-09-27 — A wave of rebuilt tables, part released and part still staged

Several dozen tables were rebuilt after real defects in the scripts that made
them. Among them: `MEFSIRODGAS_Nileksela_2023_freq` had been written from the
severity group, so it held the 499 severity respondents rather than the 501
frequency ones. `fcupanas_cffsdas_reyna_2018` pooled PANAS items 11–20 across
studies that printed them in different orders, and cut Study 3's 7-point
responses to missing; those now ship as their own `_7pt` table.
`iandolo_2021_asq` shipped three reverse-keyed items already reversed for Italy
and Japan but raw for Spain, and is now raw throughout (627 rows changed).
`quopl2_forster_2021_quop` had response times in milliseconds, not seconds. The
18 `eammi_grahe_2018_*` tables were shipping Qualtrics' whole-survey duration
as `rt` — one identical value for every item a respondent answered — which is
now `cov_survey_duration` instead. `ds14_mokken` had item Si3 overwritten with
Si1. `alsuhibani_2022_gcbs` mapped Study 2's items by position and was shifted
by one. `opladen2025_*` had collapsed eight pairs of different people who
shared an anonymised code, and now reports the 217 participants the deposit's
own summary implies.

Some of this is released and some is not, so check before assuming a fix
reached you. The `iandolo_2021_asq` and `liu_2025_ydcy` corrections are
confirmed live, at `item_response_warehouse_3` v10.0 and
`item_response_warehouse_4` v9.0. Refs #2282.

## 2026-09-27 — Congressional roll calls

Released in corpus version 442. `rollcall_house` and `rollcall_senate` treat
congressional votes from the 110th through 118th Congresses as item response
data, with `resp` 1 for Yea and 0 for Nay and members linked across Congresses
by bioguide ID. Item text for each vote is in the `irw_text_3` shard.

## 2026-09-27 — The validator checks folders, and warns about rights

`irw-validate` 1.3.0 accepts a directory and takes `-r`/`--recursive`, so you
can check a whole folder of tables rather than one file at a time. It also
names the dominant `resp` value rather than only flagging that one exists,
adds `--verbose`, and warns with the rights-register row for an instrument
before a table ships. Version 1.2.0, tagged on 2026-09-21, started checking
what an `rt` column *means* rather than only that it parses as a number. Both
went out as release tags, which is what publishes them to PyPI; the
[browser validator](validate.qmd) and `pip install -U irw-validate` run the
same checks.

## 2026-09-26 — Nominal-response tables now end in `_nom`

Corpus version 439 renamed 66 tables in the nominal source to carry a `_nom`
suffix, so that no table name is shared across two IRW sources. 52 of them are
ENEM tables. No response changed.

This matters if you refer to a nominal table by name, and it bites in two
different ways. For 59 of the 66, a core table of the same name still exists,
so the old name still resolves — but to the core table, not the nominal one
you may have meant. For the other seven, including `preference_inventory`,
`persuade_learningagency`, `goldberg_2018_spa_computer_use` and
`mthimkhulu_2023_pirls_reading_mc`, there was no core table of that name, so
the old name now resolves to nothing. The renames point both ways in the
change record. The uploader now refuses a table name another IRW source is
already using, so this particular collision should not recur. See
[the nominal data standard](nominal_standard.qmd) for what the nominal source
holds.

## 2026-09-25 — Project KIDS item names now carry the WJ-III form

Corpus versions 435 and 436. Forms A and B of the Woodcock-Johnson III put
different words and problems at the same position, and the ten Project KIDS WJ
tables had been pooling the two forms under a single item name. Item names now
carry the form, which roughly doubles the item count in each table, or more:
`project_kids_wj_lwid_wave` goes from 76 items to 228, `project_kids_wj_ap`
from 39 to 78, `project_kids_wj_mf` from 80 to 160, `project_kids_wj_pc_wave`
from 44 to 130, and so on across all ten.

If you have fit a model to one of these tables, it was treating two different
stimuli as one item wherever respondents took different forms.

## 2026-09-25 — A third item-text shard

Item text now spans `irw_text`, `irw_text_2` and `irw_text_3`; the third shard
went live in corpus version 422. Both the R and the Python package resolve all
three for you. As before, querying `irw_text` directly gets you part of the
collection, not all of it.

## 2026-09-24 — 4,495 tables, and item text for 1,589 of them

The corpus has grown from 4,273 tables in mid-September to 4,495. Many of the
new tables came from systematic sweeps of open-access journals (PLOS ONE and
Europe PMC) for articles that deposit item-level responses under an open
licence. The homepage now also shows how many tables have item text alongside
their responses: 1,589.

## 2026-09-23 — What a collection actually searched

The documented coverage of the `tagged-subset-only` collections was wrong, and
in the optimistic direction. Those collections are built by reading the
`construct name` tag — not merely "has a tags row", which is what the previous
figure of roughly 62% counted. Most rows added by auto-tagging carry no
construct name, so the real figure is about half the documented corpus: 2,467
of 4,495 tables as of 2026-09-23, and far less in the newer warehouses (98% of
the first, 77% of the second, 26% of the third, 27% of the fourth, 30% of the
fifth, 52% of the sixth). Each collection definition now states the exact
number of tables it searched, and `irw_collections()` says so in its
documentation. As the [Browse IRW Collections](collections.qmd) page already
noted, a collection is a starting point, not a census.

## 2026-09-21 — Two new vignettes

[What Is a Floor, Actually?](./vignettes/esm_floor.qmd) asks how much of the
pile-up at the bottom of experience-sampling scales is real. It measures how
much floor IRW's intensive longitudinal datasets actually carry, and compares a
censored model, a bounded-response model and a graded model on a study that
randomised its response format.
[Guessing in Multiple-Choice Data](./vignettes/guessing.qmd) compares three
published corrections for guessing against standard IRT baselines on real IRW
tables, using out-of-sample prediction, to see which correction helps and when
the correction itself does harm.

## 2026-09-19 — IRW Data Standard 1.0, and a validator that runs in your browser

[The data standard](standard.qmd) is now a numbered, versioned specification.
Clauses C1 to C7 are marked MUST or SHOULD, clause numbers will never be reused,
and every change goes in a version table at the bottom of the page. Version 1.0
is in beta while we hear from people using it outside the IRW. To check a file
against it, drop the file on the [browser validator](validate.qmd), which runs
entirely on your own computer, or run `pip install irw-validate` for the
command-line version. Both run the same checks and report each problem against
a numbered clause. The standard describes a valid table. It does not claim that
every table IRW published before 1.0 conforms.

## 2026-09-19 — A page for every table

Every table with a recorded licence now has its own page, and there is an
index of all of them at [/tables/](/tables/). That is 4,169 tables when the
pages were first built. Each page shows the table's licence in bold, repeats a
restrictive licence beside the download buttons, and gives a ready-to-copy
citation. Each page also carries schema.org and
[Croissant](https://mlcommons.org/working-groups/data/croissant/) metadata,
so Google Dataset Search and machine-learning tools can find and load
individual tables. A table without a known licence gets no page until the
licence is known. A table with an open data defect keeps its page but gets a
banner and is kept out of search results. A withdrawn table keeps its URL as a
notice that it was withdrawn.

## 2026-09-19 — Tables you download are kept on disk

R package 1.3.0 and Python package 0.3.0 keep each table they download as a
Parquet file and reuse it in later sessions, so restarting no longer
downloads the same table again. Every download counts against Redivis'
30-day export limit, so this matters. The two packages share one cache: a
table fetched in Python is not downloaded again in R.

## 2026-09-19 — A public record of corrections

IRW corrects published tables regularly, but until now nothing told you a table
you had used had changed. The new [Corrections](corrections.qmd) page states
how IRW handles it — released versions never change, a correction is a new
version, renames point both ways — and lists corrections to published
response tables, starting with those released on 2026-08-27, each with the IRW
version it took effect in and the issue that reported it. If a correction touches a table in your analysis,
`irw_use_version()` with the earlier number still returns what you had.

## 2026-09-08 — An MCP server for the IRW

The Python package now ships a local [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)
server, so an AI assistant can search the corpus, describe a table, read its
processing notes, and fetch bounded slices of data without you pasting anything
in by hand. Seven tools, all read-only. Setup instructions are on
[Using an AI Assistant](agents.qmd), alongside the plain-text
[briefing at /llms.txt](llms.txt) for assistants that cannot run a server.

`resp_raw` is now documented in [the core data standard](standard.qmd): the
column that preserves a response exactly as the source recorded it, when
`resp` had to be coerced to a number.

## 2026-09-07 — `pip install irw`

The Python package is [on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/irw/). Previously it
had to be installed from GitHub. One consequence worth knowing: `pip install
irw` gives you the last *released* version, so a fix that has been merged is
not necessarily a fix you have.

## 2026-09-05 — Item text outgrew one table, and some wording was withdrawn

Item text is now spread across shards (`irw_text`, `irw_text_2`) because a
single Redivis dataset holds at most 1000 tables. Both the R and Python
packages resolve shards for you; if you were querying `irw_text` directly, you
were seeing only part of the collection.

Separately, a rights review removed IRW-hosted item *wording* for several
instruments — including PROMIS, the TAS-20 and the DSES — where the
instrument's own licence bars redistribution, even though the response data
remains freely available. The licence on a deposited dataset is not a licence
to the instrument inside it. Response data for those tables is untouched;
only the wording is gone. R package 1.1.3 released the same day.

## 2026-09-04 — Tag coverage, and what the tags are worth

A long backfill closed the tag gap: missing tag cells went from 1,427 to 11,
published in IRW data version 20.0. Because more coverage is not the same as
more accuracy, there is now a [Tag Quality](tags_quality.qmd) page reporting
what human-versus-machine comparisons actually found — including where the
machine labels disagree with a table's own covariates. Tags are a search aid,
not a warranty.

The same day, [/llms.txt](llms.txt) went up: a single plain-text briefing on
the IRW written for AI assistants, and a [page explaining it](agents.qmd) for
the humans pointing them at it.

## 2026-09-03 — One version number for the whole corpus

Every response now carries an `irw_version`, and there is a corpus-wide
version manifest behind it. `irw_version()` / `irw_use_version()` in R and
`irw.version()` in Python let you read the current version, look up what was
current on a given date, and pin an entire analysis to one version. Version
numbers are never reused or renumbered.

Also that day: a [pilot of per-table landing pages](data.qmd) for 25 tables,
each with schema.org and Croissant metadata, so individual IRW tables can be
found and machine-read from outside the warehouse.

## 2026-09-02 — R package gains prediction utilities

`irw_imv()` and `irw_predict()` give the information-theoretic model
comparison example a home in the package rather than in a vignette. `redivis`
moved from Imports to Suggests, so installing `irw` no longer requires it
until you fetch data. `irw_simdata()`'s 2PL discriminations now have a spread
worth simulating — previously they were near-constant. Released as 1.1.0
through 1.1.2.

## 2026-08-29 — Collections

Related tables are now grouped into named collections, browsable on
[Browse IRW Collections](collections.qmd), filterable in the data explorer,
and readable from R with `irw_collections()` and `irw_collection()`. Inclusion
calls are ours and are worth verifying before you rely on one.
